text.p: Bulgaria's majority Socialists boycotted parliament on Thursday in protest at an agreement to hold an early general election, saying they were being ousted from power by undemocratic means.

Opposition deputies had just ended a boycott of their own after success following 30 days of mass protests, but with just nine Socialist deputies present, national radio said, Thursday's session to discuss income tax law lacked a quorum and could not proceed.
Socialist party sources said they planned to block all activity of the outgoing parliament, due to be dissolved by President Petar Stoyanov ready for elections due by April 20.
The Socialists said they would attend only the session to debate changes in the electoral law.
After 30 days of mass street protests fuelled by economic hardship, Stoyanov on Tuesday brokered a deal under which the Socialists agreed to give up attempts to form a government.

"For the second time in the last seven years the Union of Democratic Forces, finding itself in a parliamentary minority after free and democratic elections, has used unconstitutional actions to erase the principles of democracy and seek revenge," said a statement from the Democratic Left coalition of the Socialists and their smaller allies.

But Ivan Kostov, leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), told reporters: "The parliamentary majority wants to destabilise the country and worsen its economic situation. There is no justification for the Left's refusal to discuss changes to income tax law, for instance."

Stoyanov must appoint a caretaker cabinet which must try to keep the economy afloat and organise the elections. A presidency spokeswoman said Sofia's respected UDF mayor Stefan Sofianski was a likely candidate for caretaker prime minister.
The Socialists are deeply divided and defections are predicted from the party to a new pro-European leftist group.
The Socialists' Marxist wing has demanded that outgoing interior minister Nikolai Dobrev, the Socialists' nominee for premier, be expelled from the party for agreeing to give up forming a government.
The UDF, favourite to win a general election after the success of its month-long campaign, must also heal internal rifts and brace itself and its supporters for tough and painful economic reforms.
The national currency has fallen from 600 levs to the dollar at the beginning of the year to trade at 2,750-2,850 on the interbank market at midday on Thursday.
The collapse of the lev has caused huge losses for the state-owned Neftohim refinery, which lacks the cash to pay suppliers. Many petrol stations have closed for lack of fuel.
Almost all striking workers returned to work on Wednesday. Coal miners at Bobov Dol ended their strike on Thursday after winning a pay rise, while Pernik's miners were still negotiating.
Sofia students turned out to clear up the mess left by their roadblocks and said they would monitor their new rulers just as critically.

"We will be ready to go back in the streets if the politicians forget their promises and start their games again because we have no connections with any political parties and we have had enough of lies already," said student leader Petar Haralampiev.
